written.myAnswer: Consistency of results means repeated measurements of the same quantity under the same conditions are close to one another.
SI units use decimal multiples and submultiples, so conversions are made using powers of ten.
A systematic error shifts measurements consistently in the same direction. A random error causes unpredictable variations between measurements.
Random errors arise from unpredictable changes in conditions or limitations in measuring or reading a quantity.
Yes. Systematic error affects accuracy by consistently shifting measurements away from the true value.
Other measurement systems include MKS, CGS and the British (FPS) system.
The metre (m) is the SI base unit of length.
SI units provide a common international standard and make measurements easier to compare and communicate.
MKS uses metre, kilogram and second as its base units. SI includes these units and additional base units, and is an internationally agreed system.
The five basic SI units used in Chemistry are metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K) and mole (mol).
Derived units are formed from basic SI units. Examples are area in square metres (m²), volume in cubic metres (m³), and density in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³).
Smaller units are preferred because laboratory samples and liquid quantities are often small, making them easier to express and measure.
Using different units makes measurements difficult to compare and convert, and can cause confusion and errors.
Indigenous units include seer and maund for mass, seer or pao for volume, and gaz, foot or inch for length.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated measurements to one another.
Systematic errors can be reduced by calibrating and zero-checking instruments, using correct technique, and correcting known instrument errors.
SI units provide a common, unambiguous standard for communicating and comparing measurements, reducing errors that could compromise safety.
Yes. Measurements are both inaccurate and imprecise when they are far from the true value and not close to one another.

SI units give space-exploration teams a common standard for communicating and comparing measurements. They also reduce conversion errors that could affect spacecraft design, navigation, experiments and safety.
